interactions.summary: Jiang tests the room with the Mucius scenario, hears a student's answer, then completes the story by showing Mucius killing the wrong man, refusing to confess, and thrusting his hand into fire as proof of terrifying will.
A student reads Beatrice's move to moral contradiction: people sometimes do wrong under threat, and the distinction between absolute will and contingent will explains how coercion and consent mix.
Jiang translates Alcmaeon into an everyday moral dilemma where obedience to a father and refusal to murder collide, showing that life often forces principles into contradiction.

claims.claim: Jiang presents Mucius as the figure who acts despite uncertainty, endures the threat of torture, and proves that absolute commitment can overpower fear.
Jiang says the lesson of the Mucius story is not clever strategy but power: when someone truly believes and acts, the universe bends toward that will.
Jiang says many real decisions force principles into collision, as in Alcmaeon having to choose between obeying his father and refusing the murder of his mother.
The passage Jiang has read into the room distinguishes absolute will, which does not consent to wrong, from contingent will, which yields out of fear of worse consequences.
claims.temporal_scope: Quoted Dantean distinction read on 2026-06-15 and treated by Jiang as a live conceptual problem for the class.

signature_moments.moment: Mucius does not just endure the fire; Jiang makes him laugh through it, turning pain tolerance into a theater of will that scares a king into retreat.
signature_moments.source_phrase: while this is happening, he's laughing
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's most unforgettable image of will overpowering fear and calculation.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang sharply separates power from strategy by saying the universe bends to the actor who is willing to act, not just to the person with the cleverest plan.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this is very different from the idea of strategy
signature_moments.why_it_matters: That distinction is reusable beyond the Mucius anecdote and marks one of Jiang's core interpretive habits.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The tragic example Beatrice uses, and Jiang explains, to show how threat and duty can force one principle into violation of another.
The will that consents to wrong out of fear that resisting would bring even greater harm.
The uncompromising will that never concurs in wrongdoing even under coercive pressure.

chronology_notes.note: This June 15 packet moves from Jiang's vivid Mucius exemplar of power-as-will into Dante's more formal distinction between absolute and contingent will under coercion.
